research.topic: NASA's Swift sees a wandering black hole shredding a star

facts.text: NASA's Swift Observatory captured an orphan black hole lighting up as it devoured a star outside a distant galaxy's core.
The galaxy is about 750 million light-years away, and the black hole weighs roughly one million times the Sun.
For a few months the flare outshone its host galaxy in ultraviolet light and radiated with the light of about 10 billion Suns.
The event was identified more than 30,000 light-years from the galaxy's center.

concepts.headline: A galaxy lost track of a million-sun black hole
concepts.premise: NASA catches a wandering black hole only when it lights up while destroying a star.
concepts.whyItWorks: The cosmic disaster is instantly clear, and the true location twist earns the deadpan payoff.
concepts.punchline: Apparently, the galaxy lost track of one.

concepts.headline: One flare briefly shined like ten billion Suns
concepts.premise: A violent off-center flare exposes an otherwise invisible wandering black hole.
concepts.whyItWorks: The scale comparison creates an immediate visual and verbal escalation.
concepts.punchline: Subtle was no longer an option.

concepts.headline: NASA found a hidden black hole because it ate loudly
concepts.premise: An invisible object reveals itself by shredding a star 30,000 light-years from the expected spot.
concepts.whyItWorks: It turns an abstract detection method into a familiar caught-in-the-act joke.
concepts.punchline: The quiet neighbor finally made noise.

concepts.headline: This black hole was found on the wrong side of town
concepts.premise: Astronomers discover a massive black hole far outside the galactic center where they usually search.
concepts.whyItWorks: A simple location mismatch explains why the discovery changes how scientists hunt.

concepts.headline: A destroyed star became a black-hole alarm
concepts.premise: The tidal disruption flare gives scientists a new way to find wandering black holes.
concepts.whyItWorks: The star's destruction becomes a clean mechanism reveal instead of a list of astronomy facts.
concepts.punchline: The alarm was unfortunately the star.

selection.reason: It has the clearest cold-audience setup, strongest location twist, and most memorable deadpan payoff.

beats: Breaking news. NASA caught a wandering black hole shredding a star outside its galaxy's center.
The flare came from 750 million light-years away, powered by a black hole roughly one million Suns heavy.
For months, it outshone its entire galaxy in ultraviolet light and blazed like ten billion Suns.
Apparently, the galaxy lost track of one.
